title: 900 Letters Meant for Audrey Hepburn Went to the Wrong Woman
title_alternatives: 900 Letters Meant for Audrey Hepburn Went to the Wrong Woman
She Answered Every Letter Sent to Her by Mistake. For 22 Years.
A Typing Error in 1952 Sent 900 Letters to a Village in Yorkshire
They Wrote to a Film Star. A Retired Schoolmistress Wrote Back.
A Third of Them Kept Writing to Her After They Knew
description:
In March 1954 a letter arrived at a cottage in the North Riding of Yorkshire, addressed to A. Hepburn. The woman who opened it was called Agnes Hepburn. She was sixty-one, she had taught in a village school for thirty-four years, and she had never been to a cinema in her life.

The letter was from a fourteen-year-old girl in Lancashire. It asked whether it was frightening to be looked at by that many people. It said that the girl's mother had died in January. And near the end, in different handwriting, as though it had been added later, it asked whether things got easier.

The mistake was not mysterious. An agency in London handled the actress's correspondence from an address book, and in 1952 somebody doing three things at once had put the wrong A. Hepburn in it. The entry sat there for twenty-four years, because letters that go astray never come back and so nothing ever looked wrong from the London end.

About nine hundred letters arrived at that cottage between 1954 and 1976. Agnes answered every one of them, in the same order every time. First: you have written to the wrong person. Second: I am sorry, or I am glad, about the thing you told me. Third: here is the correct address in London, in full. And fourth — the part that turned an administrative error into whatever this was — if the letter had asked a question that a person could answer, she answered it herself, at length, as herself.

She was never pretending to be anybody. Every surviving reply says so in the first line.

About a third of them wrote back to her anyway, after they had the right address.

This story is a work of fiction. Agnes, the agency, the archive and every detail in it are invented, created for storytelling and not drawn from any record.
